hints: Look at what type of structure each oxide has, giant lattice or small separate molecules, because that controls melting point.
Remember that $\text{SiO}_2$ is a giant covalent network while $\text{SO}_2$ is simple molecular, so one needs much more energy to melt.
For $\text{NH}_3$ versus $\text{PH}_3$, ask which one can form hydrogen bonds between its molecules and what that does to boiling point.
walkthrough:
**Check Statement 1 - Type of Structure**

Think about how the particles are held together. $\text{SiO}_2$ forms a giant covalent lattice with strong covalent bonds in all directions, while $\text{SO}_2$ exists as small discrete molecules held by weak van der Waals forces.

**Compare Melting Points for Statement 1**

Melting $\text{SiO}_2$ means breaking many strong covalent bonds, which needs huge energy and a very high temperature (around 1600 C). Melting $\text{SO}_2$ only means overcoming weak intermolecular forces, so it melts very easily.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{giant covalent} >> \text{simple molecular in melting point}$$

**Check Statement 2 - Intermolecular Forces**

Both $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{PH}_3$ are simple molecular hydrides. Focus on the special force in ammonia. N is small and very electronegative with a lone pair, so $\text{NH}_3$ forms hydrogen bonds between molecules.

**Compare Boiling Points for Statement 2**

$\text{PH}_3$ cannot hydrogen bond because P is larger and less electronegative, so it has only weaker permanent dipole and van der Waals forces. Hydrogen bonding is much stronger, so $\text{NH}_3$ needs more energy to boil and has the higher boiling point.

So both statement 1 and statement 2 are correct.

options.A: Both statements are true. Statement 1 is true because giant covalent $\text{SiO}_2$ has a far higher melting point than simple molecular $\text{SO}_2$. Statement 2 is true because $\text{NH}_3$ has hydrogen bonding while $\text{PH}_3$ does not, giving ammonia the higher boiling point.
options.B: This says only statement 1 is correct and rejects statement 2. That is a trap if you forget hydrogen bonding or think boiling point follows Group 5 size trend. $\text{NH}_3$ is the exception because of strong $\text{N-H...N}$ hydrogen bonds.
options.C: This says only statement 2 is correct and rejects statement 1. That is a trap if you think both oxides are simple molecular because both contain a non-metal and oxygen. $\text{SiO}_2$ is actually giant covalent, like diamond, not molecular like $\text{CO}_2$ or $\text{SO}_2$.
options.D: This says neither statement is correct. That would mean misunderstanding both structure types and intermolecular forces. Both comparisons are classic examples of strong bonding or hydrogen bonding raising melting and boiling points.
